div.head: Wal 1
div.ab: Wealreaf (id est mortuum refare) est opus niðingi: si quis negare uelit, faciat hoc cum XLVIII tainis plene nobilibus.
Walreaf is niðinges dǽde: gif hwá ofsacen wille, do þæt mid eahta ⁊ feowertig fulbórenra þegena.
Leichenberaubung ist That eines [Fried- und] Ehrlosen: wenn es einer ableugnen will, thue er das mit [Eideshilfe von] 48 vollgeborenen Thegnas.
Robbing a corpse is the deed of a nithing [a man without peace or honour]: if anyone wishes to deny it, let him do so with [the oath-help of] 48 fully-born thegns.
Robbing the slain is a villianous act; if anyone wishes to deny it, let him do so with [the help of] 48 noble-born thegns.

note.label: possibly related
note.quote: might the Wantage provision that corpses of executed thieves could be 'taken up' … (III 7 – 7:1), conceivably have been construed as a licence

note.label: matches
note.quote: the Wantage demand that accusations … be cleared with 'three twelves' match the Walreaf stipulation that this outlaw's deed be answered with an oath of forty-eight

div.note: The Latin is the Quadripartitus; Liebermann's Old English is from H (Textus Roffensis f. 32v, after Ordal, same hand, c. 1120; perhaps a fragment of a law, after c. 910 because of Norse influence). Liebermann explains ‘niðing’ as ‘worthless, wretched man’. In the Quadripartitus it follows Pax; IV Atr follows it. K: a stray opening bracket before ‘XLVIII’ removed. Clause number 1 added (this text has a single clause). Liebermann compares I Cn 3 and 6.2a (MS A).; BQ: page of each of Liebermann’s texts and of his German, checked against Liebermann, Gesetze I (column heads, read twice), October 2026 (e.g. was “(empty)”, now “Q 393; H 392; German 393”; 1 rows of Wal)
